# Top 5 posts from r/MovieSuggestions day

## 1. Movie Night with my buddies… looking for something that’ll leave us speechless.

**Score:** 86
**Body:** Looking for any weird/creepy movies that are good but will leave you thinking “WTF did I just watch”. Looking for something in the horror/thriller genre but anything that comes to mind will work. Let me know if you have any suggestions! Thanks guys!

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Very bad things 
2. Oldboy, the original korean version from 2003.     
Or, also from Korea, The Wailing
3. Midsommar
4. Mandy
5. The Descent 
6. Some of the most realistic gore in the horror/thriller genre. A really compelling suspenseful story. Interesting cast of characters:
- Green room room (2015) <- punks fight Nazis
- Blue ruin (2013) <- clumsy revenge
7. The Greasy Strangler
8. Not horror, but Sorry to Bother You is great, and about as what-the-fuck as something can get
9. Check out House (1977).
10. The Lobster. The whole movie, those three letters were just circling in my head: WTF? WTF! WTF?!?

## 2. Movies like heavy metal

**Score:** 30
**Body:** I would love to watch more movies like Heavy Metal that are really artsy or like a long music video lol. By the way, don't watch the sequel; it is ass. Please dont suggest fantasia or fantasia 2000

### Top 9 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Ralph Bakshi's movies
  - American Pop definitely fits the bill
2. Interstella 5555 by Daft Punk
3. Not animated, but Mandy sure is artsy and feels like a long music video lol. Also, there's metal. So yeah
  - Second time I'm seeing Mandy recommended today, and it makes me happy. I love that movie. 
4. Fire and Ice (1983)

The Spine of Night (2021)
5. It's not musical, but Fantastic Planet (early 70s) is pretty out there!

ETA: It's also animated.
6. Rock & Rule (1983)
7. Gandahar + Fantastic Planet 
8. The Wall. Bakshi movies. 

## 3. Any good Horror superhero films besides Brightburn and The Crow?

**Score:** 25
**Body:** Any good Horror movies with a comic book story or superhuman story besides the ones mentioned? 

I guess Chronicle would also fit the bill. Really looking for more similar to Brightburn or The Crow though.

### Top 9 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Blade?
  - Oh, totally.  Blade.  

"Some motherfuckers are always trying to ice-skate uphill."
2. Spawn
3. Hellboy (2004)
4. Sam Rami's Darkman
  - First film I thought of, it's basically Phantom of the Opera crossed with The Shadow
5. The New Mutants
6. Darkman!

Also Blade, Constantine, and Hellboy. New Mutants too, but your mileage may vary on that one. And I suppose Clayface comes out in a month.

Split and Glass are follow-ups to Unbreakable which is a take on superhero movies.

If you consider horror movies built around superpowers close enough, there’s Carrie, Doctor Sleep, Firestarter, Scanners, and The Fury
7. I mean technically you could count Unbreakable, Split & Glass.
8. "Dr. Strange & The Multiverse of Madness" was directed by Sam Raimi (of Evil Dead fame) and gives a bit of a horror vibe.

Speaking of Dr. Strange, Charles Band was supposed to direct a Dr. Strange film in the eighties. The license expired, so the film was repurposed into Dr. Mordrid.

## 4. Can you recommend me a film/documentary about an eccentric and fun character?

**Score:** 23
**Body:** I've recently been on a binge watching a lot of documentaries. I watched Exit Through the Giftshop and American Movie back to back. Absolutely flawless, I loved every second of it.

So I'm wondering if there are any documentaries or films in that kind of vein. Very comedic and also extremely fun to watch with friends.

I would love to organize a watch party with my friend group and watch something like that. So any and all recommendations are welcome!

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. The wild and wonderful whites of West Virginia.

Heads up that it’s also pretty dark and some parts are depressing, but it’s such a fun and fascinating watch in my opinion. 
2. *That Guy Who Was In That Thing* isn’t about one single person, it’s about character actors, and focuses on several that you’ve probably seen in multiple TV shows and/or movies without knowing their names.

*Herb Alpert Is…* Alpert is maybe not as quirky as, say, Banksy, but he’s an interesting guy: seventh richest musician in the world, was the A in A&M Records, and is the only person to have a #1 single as both a singer and an instrumentalist. He’s also currently still touring at age 91.
3. Grey Gardens - both the documentary and Hollywood version
4. Herzog rules at this.   
*Grizzly Man* and *My Best Fiend* are favorites
5. Jim & Andy: The Great Beyond 

It's about Jim Carrey portraying Andy Kaufman in the movie, Man on The Moon. It was a lot of fun.
6. The Pee Wee Herman documentary on HBO is pretty great: Pee-Wee As Himself

Cutie And The Boxer (2013) is odd and fun.
7. Crumb
8. Jiro Dreams of Sushi, just a slow look at a Michelin star chef in his sushi stand in a Tokyo subway station, and everything it takes to make the perfect sushi roll
9. Tiger King

Last Stop Lerrimah-This one has a unique premise. 11 people are the only residents in a very remote town in Australia. One goes missing and the rest of the town are each viable suspects of possible foul play. All of them are eccentric characters like something straight out of a Cohen Bros movie.
10. Bernie - not a documentary, a 2011 movie based on real person/events with Jack Black in the title role

## 5. Looking for a movie like Ex-Machina

**Score:** 19
**Body:** I'm looking for a sci-fi with a really unpredictable story and a twist that I won't see coming. Any recommendations on what to watch?

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. *Moon* maybe?

*Upgrade* is more of an action sci-fi. It's not super unpredictable, but still might qualify.

It is hard to recommend movies with twists because just knowing it has a twist might ruin it 😅
2. I always think of Ex Machina, Arrival, and Her together.  Three really smart, slightly downbeat SF films that came out within a couple years of each other.
3. Midnight Special 
4. Westworld
5. Definitely give Companion a watch. 
6. Stepford Wives (the original)
7. Upgrade 
8. I am Mother (2019)  
9. Cypher (2002)
10. Under The Skin

# Top 5 posts from r/moviecritic day

## 1. Edward Norton was in an insane run during late 1990s

**Score:** 2216
**Body:** Top image: American History X (1998)

Middle image: Primal Fear (1996)

Bottom image: Fight Club (1999)

### Top 7 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. The craziest part of this was that Primal Fear was his first ever role. 


  - That’s a wild fact that’s hard to believe. Also hard to believe they would hire someone from an open audition with absolutely no film credits. Did he even have an agent? 
    - No agent he just smashed it at the audition. They were having trouble casting the main role. Leonardo DiCaprio had rejected the role so they went through auditions with many. A friend of Edward Norton was going for a different role in this movie and told Norton to audition for Aaron. He was working in a new york theater before this role. When he entered the audition he changed the accent to kentucky like and made the stuttering Aaron. The casting directors were left speechless and casted him through that.

So his talent did that for him with no agent
    - I saw an interview with Richard Gere about this. 

They were really struggling to cast the role, so they did an open call. Norton had a friend who had auditioned for another part tell him the open call was happening. He walked in, in character already, and auditioned in NYC, and the casting director thought he was terrific. So they flew him out to audition with Richard, and he was amazing. But then they all realized he had literally done nothing, and they got a bit scared it was a fluke. So they had him read again with Richard, and they thought he was even better than the last time. 

The audition tape got so much buzz that he was cast by Woody Allen in Everybody Says I Love you and by Forman in The People v Larry Flynt before Primal Fear was even released.

It was such a ballsy move to cast him. I seriously doubt whether that would happen today.


  - He deserved an Oscar for that acting.
2. I hate the fact that everyone ignores 25th Hour, to me it’s a top 5 Norton performance
3. Also great in Rounders (1998).
4. The Score (2001) was pretty good also. I know it's isn't 90's but it was close enough to count in my book.
5. Death to Smoochy  
NO love for this amazing movie?
6. Even past that period!  Wasn't super crazy about Red Dragon as a film, doesn't touch Silence of the Lambs for me, but damn he was pretty phenomenal in that

## 4. Anyone else obsessed with these trashy Y2K cult movies?

**Score:** 181
**Body:** Am I the only one who thinks there was a very specific type of movie that basically existed from the late 90s to the mid-2000s?

I'm talking about movies like *Jawbreaker*, *Cruel Intentions*, *Teaching Mrs. Tingle*, *Sugar & Spice*, *The Faculty*, *American Psycho 2*, Carrie 2, *The Butterfly Effect*, and *Jennifer's Body*.

They're all pretty different on paper, but they somehow give me the exact same vibe.

They all have that glossy Y2K aesthetic, over-the-top fashion, dark humor, ridiculously dramatic teenagers, and this weird dreamlike atmosphere where nobody acts like a real person. Everyone is either a sociopath, a manipulator, or one bad day away from committing a felony.

A lot of these movies got mixed reviews when they came out, but years later they've become cult classics. They're campy, stylish, kind of trashy in the best possible way, and way more memorable than a lot of "better" movies from the same era.

I don't really think of them as teen comedies, thrillers, or horror movies. They feel like their own weird little genre that Hollywood was making for a few years and then suddenly stopped.

I've jokingly been calling it things like: Y2K Teen Trash Cinema, Teen Sleaze Noir, Millennial Camp Thrillers

Does anyone else know what I'm talking about? And what other movies would you put in this category?

Because I'm convinced there are like 20-30 movies that all share this exact energy. I also wonder why some of them became cult movies whereas other became so forgotten like American Psycho 2. I mean, that movie is really terrible but I had so much fun watching it, I feel like it's very campy and cringeworthy but it's enjoyable in some strange way.

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Cruel intentions is my all time favourite movie and has been since I stumbled across it when I was 9. 

I work in film, I watch a ton, and nothing has ever come close to dethroning it. It’s got everything! 

Side note, we need to bring back the Hollywood Hangup 
2. I love these movies so much.

To add to your list Disturbing Behavior is one and so is The Skulls as well as Gossip! I also feel like Cry Wolf and Urban Legends fit the bill. While the last 2 trend more into horror thrillers, they still have that vibe completely. You might also like the Buffy the Vampire Slayer movie (not TV show), since it truly is this weird 80s horror vibe mixed with this 90s high school sarcasm for lack of a better word that you're talking about.
3. Yes, love all those. I would add The In Crowd, Gossip, Freeway, Devil in the Flesh, The Rules of Attraction, Swimfan, Go, The Skulls, O
  - Abandon got me so into Charlie Hunnam waay before SOA. The Doom Generation, Nowhere, Mysterious Skin from Gregg Araki all so good. Bully. Cherry Falls. There's this crazy low budget one Vampire Clan based on a true story but so trashy.. so many hidden gems
4. Empire Records ticks all the boxes. Dramatic, sociopathic teenagers especially.
5. Idle hands fits this!
6. Is y2k a Gen Z term? Cause back then y2k was literally the year 2000. After 2000 we stopped using y2k 
7. The Butterfly Effect is one of the most underrated (by critics) movies of all time. I remember it having a RT score of like 18%. 

Another movie that really flopped from this era but is a complete banger is Stay with Ewan McGregor and Ryan Gosling.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. 25th Hour (2002) is one of Spike Lee's finest achievements. This film honestly depicted the mood of post-9/11 New York City, the confusion and simmering rage

**Score:** 84
**Body:** Edward Norton plays Monty, a convicted drug dealer about to start a seven-year prison sentence. The movie follows how he spends his final hours of freedom.

Instead of this rah-rah "*USA, USA"* patriotism some other filmmakers might've shown, Spike Lee captured the feeling of collective anger and grief that was still fresh among the citizens. Revisiting this film, I'm still struck by how it depicts a society that was coldly awoken to the illusion of security. One critic wrote that "25th Hour is as much an urban historical document as Rossellini's Open City, filmed in the immediate aftermath of the Nazi occupation of Rome".

How do we grapple with the choices we made, and what will we do with the time we have left? Tomorrow is not guaranteed.

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. While this is far from the best movie I've ever seen, randomly stumbling onto this movie on HBO way back in like 2005 late at night is one of my favorite movie memories. I was a huge Ed Norton and PSH fan.  It sucked me in, the vibe of the whole film, and the ending of this movie is to this day the best endings of a movie I've ever seen. It really kicked off a love affair with movies for me.  I haven't seen in in like 20 years I still think about it all the time.  I think i will watch it this weekend and see if it holds up at all for me.
  - I watch it every couple years and it definitely holds up
2. The soundtrack is amazing, so dark and fits the mood perfectly.

25th hour isn't the greatest movie and is certainly not without its flaws, yet its the type of movie that stays with you for a long time after watching.
3. Norton has his legendary rant, its very good. I cant think of another movie that capture ground zero so soon, quite like this - i think that alone makes this an important time capsule 
4. I read the novel of The 25th Hour before it was published because we reviewed it and had an interview with David Benioff the author. 

He negotiated to adapt his own novel into a screenplay and The 25th Hour is both a very readable novel and an excellent screenplay and film.

He went on to adapt and create Game of Thrones for HBO.
  - The his and City of Thieves are his best work.
  - Oh! TIL.

Excellent film, by the way. Spike Lee is such an uneven film maker, but this is one of his best.
5. I saw it when it came out, and again several times over the years. It’s honestly one of those movies that somehow becomes better and more poignant as time goes on and you have the benefit of perspective because you’re no longer living in that place in time. 

Incredible film. 

## 2. How do you feel about the length of Drive My Car (2021)?

**Score:** 49
**Body:** By the end of the film, I was really enjoying Drive My Car. But it took a looooonnnggg time to get there, and I'm still not sure why it had to be almost 3 hours. What's your take on this?

The main parts where it lost me were the theatre rehearsal scenes, which take up a significant amount of time. I generally enjoy slow films, but the rehearsal scenes didn't seem slow, as much as stationary. What are these scenes really about? I just felt like I was watching some actors, playing actors, rehearsing a play, but with no idea why. But did they work for you? And what would you say is their importance to the film as a whole? 

I also find it impossible to get invested in stories within stories. That made it hard for me to draw connections between the story of the play and the story of the film. That could just be me though. Another difficulty is that I've heard of Chekov's play Uncle Vanya, but I know literally nothing about it. I was wondering if the film assumes a degree of familiarity that I don't have? 

The main things I took from the film were the fantastic performances, cinematography, and the details of Japanese life. So it was well worth a watch. But it felt to me like a 2-hour film that took 3 hours. 

Looking forward to hearing everyone's opinions on this - particularly people who loved it and want to talk about what I was missing.



### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. The film is open to interpretation in a lot of ways but I’d say: The point of the rehearsal scenes is to show the process of introspection in a somewhat cinematic way. 

For a slow art house film, Drive My Car has a very explicit “this is the theme of the movie” monologue near the end: we will never fully understand others, but if we try really hard and put the work in, we can understand ourselves, and doing that will give us a better understanding of the world. The protagonist never fully understood his wife, that’s what the whole film is about, and he doesn’t seem to have any answers to help his actors understand their characters in Uncle Vanya either. The actors ask him for clarity and direction, and essentially his answer is always “I don’t know or don’t want to influence you, but if you read the text again and focus only on yourself and what you’re doing, maybe that will help give you an understanding of the play.” It’s ironic in the sense that he spends most of the film refusing to do that same introspection, he’s in the car listening over and over to other people’s words futilely believing they will make him understand another person better. I do think this kind of demands to be read in a metaphorical way, because if you take it very literally, he’s probably a bad director and essentially is asking his actors to do the work of directing themselves for him because he’s too lost in his own grief to do his job. That’s a reading I think you can make, but I can’t imagine Hamaguchi was going for something so cynical, the movie feels fundamentally hopeful and uplifting. 

Not even addressing the content of Uncle Vanya as a play about grief, the production within the movie is built around a central gimmick of all actors speaking a different language. They cannot communicate with each other and so they’re forced to focus only on themselves and what they are reading (I’ve watched this movie with people who didn’t get that aspect, I guess it’s subtle or it all blends together after a while and people forget Korean and Japanese are different languages?). In universe this is a cutesy coming together thing, but in the context of the film it’s another layer of people not being able to understand each other, but by putting in the work to better understand themselves (reading the text over and over until they know other people’s cues even though they don’t know the words being spoken to them), they get a better sense of the big picture. 
2. Pretty much all of the things that you didn't like were things I personally loved about the movie. It's my clear #1 or #2 movie of 2021 (along with Hamaguchi's other film that year).

I had a cursory knowledge at best of Vanya, but I never felt in the dark or missing some reference (though I'm sure a deeper understanding of the play would add another layer). The characters' actions and reactions on the screen told the story. If you want reflections from the story within the story, grief, guilt, and a general existential ennui are pretty clear ones to me.

I personally love movies about movies, plays, productions, etc. One of my favorite sub-genres.

I was totally engrossed the entire movie - it never felt slow or long to me. Perfectly paced. I was constantly interested in what was happening on screen. What hour of film would you cut from this movie? I can't imagine what you would think of Happy Hour.

Hamaguchi's pacing, his patience, his ability to let his story breathe are some of his best traits. It's not a movie concerned with hitting you with story beats by a certain page. You say it felt like a 2 hour movie that took 3 hours, but if you cut this movie down by an hour it's an entirely different movie. Completely wipes out the novelistic approach that Hamaguchi is so skilled at and a core part of what makes the movie so powerful.
  - Same here. This was such a sweeping emotional epic that it totally earned its 3 hour runtime. Usually long movies start to drag for me if they're over-plotted (like a lot of action blockbusters these days), but Drive My Car just had so much to say about the characters and the settings that it never felt indulgent to me. Plus it's cobbling together like 2-3 Murakami short stories as well as a whole lot of original material that it kind of needs a long runtime to fit the different sections in.
  - «Clear #1 or #2 movie» is a pretty funny phrase
    - True! I just meant that those 2 were my clear Top 2 of 2021, but I alternate between which of the two is my favorite.
3. It is, to me, a perfect movie. It feels the way reading Haruki Mirukami feels. It moves at the deliberate pace of someone speaking emphatically in sign language. My wife doesn’t always go in for long movies, but after I showed it to her she said “that was one of the better movies you’ve had me watch.” 
4. To me, Hamaguchi is interested actors and performance. Even his shorter films like *Wheel of Fortune and Fantasy* feel like mini-plays. In ep 1 for example, we have a long dialogue scene in a car, then a long dialogue scene in an office. *Asako I and II* has an actor playing two roles. The actor has to play double duty. All his films feel like acting exercises (*Happy Hour* was born from an acting workshop) that just somehow have extended and expanded to film.  
  
That being said, I am not knowledgeable in theatre or Chekov and admittedly I still haven't read or seen *Uncle Vanya* since I saw *Drive My Car*. I have read that there are parallels between the play and the film, such as Yoon-a (the Korean woman) mirroring the character she plays, Sonya and other sorts of echoes... but this came after I had seen the film and still without knowledge of the entirety of the play itself.  
  
So as someone uneducated in *Uncle Vanya*, I ended up becoming interested in other things more than the play's content. I got a glimpse of maybe, *maybe,* how Hamaguchi himself works with actors. I thought about how if one doesn't understand what someone literally says because they speak a different language, can one still infer the meaning? (I'm definitely interested in seeing his latest *All of a Sudden* with these thoughts in mind.) I thought about this in regards to his wife who communicates via a long improvised dream-like narrative post-sex as if that is her private language to him... and then he finds out that she has spoken than same language to someone else. I thought about how the play itself has become a way of connecting with his wife and so when she has passed away he still listens to her within the context of work. I thought about theatre and performance to a paying audience and theatre and performance we do to each other.

I thought about the time given to different characters even when their actual roles within *Drive My Car* is small and what we learn through their audition. It's not a complete surprise that Takatsuki turns out to be a bad person considering his audition felt aggressive. I learn a little about Janice as a character when she challenges Kafuku's directing methods even though Janice is not given much screen time. When Janice and Yoon-a have a moment in their acting exercise outdoors, it's a language that no one is able to penetrate. Takatsuki does not understand it and Kafuku says only they understand it - so perhaps Janice now understands what Kafuku had been trying to do during those readings.  
  
I thought about I see how Kafuku works as a director and as actor. Instead of characters telling me he's great etc. I actually see how he works and when others question him, he tells them to still do the method. As a director he can give demands. As a performer, and as someone facing the emotions and enacting the emotions (something he had been trouble doing since his wife's passing) he struggles until the very end of the film.

And then we have Yoon-a's final lines as Sonya: *We'll live through the long, long days, and through the long nights. We'll patiently endure the trials that fate sends our way \[...\] And then at last, we shall rest. I believe it. I strongly believe it from the bottom of my heart. When that time comes, we shall rest.* There's meaning in these words in the play and in the film and in our reality.

A bit of a ramble and maybe a little disjointed but those had been my thoughts at the time of seeing the film.
5. This is my favorite movie. Hamaguchi's movies are, for me, the closest I feel to being able to inhabit a work of literature. The way I see it, Hamaguchi is really a theater director and literary writer who happens to make movies, and the way he paces scenes is very similar to how they would feel as live theater. This is most apparent in Wheel of Fortune and Fantasy, where we barely even get camera moves. I find the effect enchanting and immersive. There's so much breathing room where you can see the micro-interactions between the actors and the environment and each other. Something I also don't see talked about enough is the excellent sound design in all of his films, which really pulls you in. 

The rehearsal scenes in Drive My Car are especially interesting once you know that the actors in the film actually used the rehearsal method. The BTS documentary shows them sitting on the ground in a circle, slowly reading through the lines out loud without emotion. One of the actors tells the interviewer "I thought it was pretty weird, but I think he might be some kind of genius".
6. I agree with the other comments so far with respect to the themes of (failures of) communication and what we learn of the characters through their behavior in the rehearsal scenes.

I want to additionally chime in that I think what we learn about the characters of Uncle Vanya and the trajectory of its story through their repeated appearance in the film really enriches what's going on with the characters of Drive My Car. IMO two of the most psychologically fascinating moves in the film are Yusuke casting Koji as Vanya (despite Koji auditioning for a different role) and Yusuke's refusal until the end of the movie to play Vanya. Caveat that I went in knowing nothing about Uncle Vanya and could be totally off-base because everything I know is inferred from Drive My Car.

Regarding "repeated appearance", bits of Uncle Vanya (recording, audition, rehearsal, performance) appear in a subjective chronology determined by their significance to the characters of Drive My Car (most frequently yusuke). Scenes are constructed so that snippets of Chekhov's words seem to function as suggestive commentary. To me this was a useful reflection of the mental state of the characters, as in: these are the parts of the play that are currently very resonant to them.

For the bulk of the movie, Yusuke appears to be very close Vanya's bitterness, his feeling of loss/wasted potential, his impotent rage. I got the sense that he saddled Koji with the character of Vanya in a conscious attempt to force him to embody these feelings in himself (that Koji likely amplified by reminding him of the situation with Oto, his wife). The old and jaded character of Vanya vs the younger and sexually vigorous character Koji showed up to play have clear parallels to Yusuke and Koji and what Yusuke does feels cathartic but also perverse. In essence: he exerts his directorial power in the face of Koji's career vulnerability to take the wind out of the sails of the energy that Koji brought into the audition (likely associated with his past controversy, we later learn) and the specter of his past robustness with his Oto.

This of course doesn't do much to help Yusuke actually move past these feelings. At least not directly: obliviously Koji probably provides the impetus for confronting his relationship with his wife as well as some additional context, and then ultimately somewhat forces Yusuke's hand by being unable to perform (a tragic outcome that I would argue Yusuke as director had a hand in). Prior to that Yusuke claims to listen to the recordings of Oto to learn the play inside and out, but their nature forces him to actively (if not always verbally) fill in for Vanya (whose lines are missing) in addition to existing in this suspended space of post-mortem engagement with his wife.

As an extension of this, when the ending of the play does come up now and then its more optimistic tone feels hollow - until the end when Yusuke is performing for an audience. A lot of credit to how this last recitation is depicted and given room to breathe, but what made it land for me was all the prior exposure and context that Hamaguchi put into place.
7. I mean, if you hate stories within stories, that's a perfectly acceptable personal quirk of taste, but it's rather odd consideration to bring to analyzing a film.  This is a natural and expected and generally satisfying part of human storytelling. Would you wander up to Shakespeare and tell him to cut that extra story out of Hamlet or Midsummers Night Dream?  Should Kurosawa pick a single point of view character for Rashomon?  Should Birdman not exist?  Or, to pick a film in conversation with with Drive My Car, should Vanya on 42nd Street  not have been made?

Nor, as an artform, do films have a natural length, even if as a boring matter of economics roughly 90 minutes to two hours is ideal for making money.  But it would hardly be unusual for, say a stage play or Broadway musical to go for three hours.  
  
Structurally, practicing the play is a way to force the director to face the grief he has buried.  We spend time with this, both because that's how grief works, and also because this isn't a pathetic paint by the numbers franchise flick, where an idiot protagonist has an epiphany-shaped story beat and says "I guess my uncle was right, with great power comes great responsibility", or some such, in the course of a single scene. 

It's perfectly fine if this film is, accidently, not something you are disposed to like.  And it's great you can find interesting things in it and are curious about what you're not getting.  But basically, it's just  a slow film about slowly coming to terms with grief that happens to employ a hallowed structure that you happen not to like.

## 5. I watched Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter... and Spring (2003). Here are my thoughts

**Score:** 5
**Body:** Beautifully shot. Simplifies the story of life almost to a contrived degree. Yet it is effective. It works. Simply due to its setting in a Buddhist monastery. The use of Buddhist teaching as a medium to tell the simplified tale of life makes it an endearing watch. Because the actions are simple, yet they are presented not from a judgmental perspective. They become simply a part of the life cycle.

Spring welcomes budding flowers. Raw in nature, innocent, ignorant, full of mistakes unknown to them. The master imparts his teachings to make a better human out of the apprentice.

Summer transforms the flower into a fruit. Ready to ripen. Feelings are expressed; love blossoms. It's human nature to have desires, and to reap all the pleasures from them and bear all the sufferings therefore.

Autumn comes; old leaves must fall, so that young may sprout later on. 

The harshness of winter turns the apprentice into the master, wise, knowledgeable, experienced; yet, he still has to bear the burden of all the guilt he has accumulated in his life. The suffering continues; his temperament towards it has matured.

Another spring comes, and the cycle repeats itself.

The movie is full of symbolism. Different animals are associated with different seasons. The puppy symbolises the joy and innocence of youth. The chicken represents greed. The cat represents purity. The fish, frog and snake are lower life forms who bear the suffering imparted by the apprentice. There is a gate to the monastery, but it has no walls, as it does not serve as a barrier. It has demons and angels drawn on it on the outside and inside, respectively, symbolising the contrast between the world outside - full of desires and suffering; and the world inside - one of equanimity. Almost all the shots are asymmetrical, referring to the imperfection and the high-and-low nature of life.

Despite all the knowledge of good and bad, the protagonist still errs, causing more suffering in the world; and he must come to terms with his wrongdoings. There is no penance, no absolution, no salvation. The guilt and suffering will always be there.
